kinds.d: Fresh sweet orange, organised by navel, Valencia and other cultivars and their protected origins.

x.d: Seedless navel orange from a Bahia, Brazil, mutation; Washington trees reached Riverside, California, in 1873.

v.d: Red-fleshed navel found at Hacienda Caracara, Valencia, Venezuela; likely a bud sport of Washington navel

x.d: Late-season juicing orange catalogued in England in 1865 as Excelsior after import from the Azores.

Developed by Palestinian farmers near Jaffa in Ottoman Palestine as a mutation of the Baladi orange from about the 1840s; practically seedless, sweet, oval, thick easy-peel skin that suits export but yields little juice.
x.dt: oval · thick skin · few seeds · poor juice, stores well

v.d: Fruit carrying the Jaffa label first marketed in 1870

x.d: Small, juicy early-season juice orange found in Florida in 1879 that replaced the older Parson Brown.

kinds.d: Red-fleshed sweet orange, mainly Sicilian Moro, Tarocco and Sanguinello.

x.d: Deepest-red blood orange, a bud mutation of Sanguinello Moscato from Lentini, Sicily.
Lighter-pigmented Sicilian blood orange, a mutation of Sanguinello and Italy's most popular table orange.
Full-blood Sicilian orange close to Moro in character.
Multi-cultivar PGI for blood oranges (Tarocco, Moro, Sanguinello) from eastern Sicily.

kinds.d: Fresh mandarin or tangerine other than clementine and satsuma, including mandarin hybrids sold as mandarins.

x.d: Large bumpy Japanese mandarin hybrid of Kiyomi x Ponkan, sold in the US as Sumo Citrus.

v.d: US brand; first sold early 2011, budwood imported 1998
Only fruit above 13 degrees Brix and under 1.0% acid may be sold as dekopon

x.d: Mandarin-pomelo hybrid and parent of Dancy and Dekopon.
Mandarin x sweet orange hybrid (tangor).

v.d: Seedless irradiated selection of Murcott from the University of California Citrus Breeding Program

x.d: King x Willowleaf cross developed by H. B. Frost.
Ponkan x hybrid mandarin; the most common US tangerine until the 1970s.
Mandarin that originated in Morocco (Afourer), with deep orange easy-peel skin, sweet-tart juicy segments, typically seedless when isolated.
x.dt: deep orange, easy-peel · sweet-tart · seedless in isolation

kinds.d: Small seedless, easy-peel mandarin type sold as clementine.

x.d: Mandarin x sweet orange hybrid from Misserghin, Algeria, named after Clément Rodier in 1902.

v.d: Mutation of Fina; most widely planted clementine in Spain

m: Clementinas de las Tierras del Ebro o Clementines de les Terres de l'Ebre PGI

kinds.d: Loose-skinned, seedless mandarin type sold as satsuma or mikan.

x.d: Most widely grown satsuma, taken to the US in 1878; the base for most other satsuma cultivars.
Early Japanese satsuma, one of three cultivars making nearly half of Japan's output.
Early Japanese satsuma, one of the three leading Japanese satsuma cultivars.
Leading Japanese satsuma cultivar.

m: 香川小原紅早生みかん GI

kinds.d: Fresh grapefruit, white or red fleshed.

x.d: Seedless white grapefruit that arose before 1862 as a root sprout in Florida; the cultivar that eclipsed Duncan.
Red grapefruit from a Thompson mutation in McAllen, Texas; sold also as Redblush.

v.d: Same type found in McAllen in 1931

x.d: Intensely red grapefruit developed by irradiating Hudson seed; released by Texas A&I.
Texas budsport from Ruby Red descent in 1976; the leading red grapefruit alongside Flame.
Red grapefruit from a Ruby Red mutation near Houston, released by USDA in 1987.

kinds.d: Fresh pomelo (pummelo), the large thick-skinned citrus.

x.d: Very large nearly spherical pomelo that reached Japan via Taiwan in 1920; record fruit 4.86 kg at Yatsushiro, Kumamoto.

brands.d: US trade name for the Dekopon mandarin, first sold in early 2011 from budwood imported in 1998.
California-based citrus growers' co-operative marketing fresh oranges, lemons and grapefruit.
Privately held US grower whose Wonderful Citrus unit sells Halos mandarins and Sweet Scarletts grapefruit.
South African citrus export brand of fresh oranges and other citrus.

notes: Orange list trimmed to cultivars with retrieved pages (Washington navel, Valencia) plus flat GIs. Not confirmed by any retrieved page and so left out as archetypes: Lane Late, Hamlin, Shamouti/Jaffa, Nadorcott, Ortanique, Setoka, Beni Madonna, Kanpei, Marisol, Thong Dee, Nam Roi (Vietnamese GIs kept flat), Oroblanco/Sweetie, Mikkabi, Arida, Ehime mikan GIs (Wikipedia does not list these as cultivars). Cara Cara kept as a version of Washington navel because Wikipedia says it is a likely bud sport.
